extracted.intended_audience: readers and potential contributors to The Popular Science Monthly (general scientific/public audience; authors of light/scientific sketches and correspondence)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and selection criteria for contributions to a magazine department titled 'Entertaining Varieties' and editorial guidance on practical approaches to studying mind (physiological vs metaphysical), plus related correspondence standards (biblical translation, copyright).

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertaining Varieties — scope and submission intent
rubrics_metrics.description: The new department 'Entertaining Varieties' is intended as a modified form of the feuilletons: it will consist of readable miscellaneous fragments of all sorts, but is not intended to be limited to mere fugitive things; it may afford a place for continuous papers of a light and entertaining kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributions should be readable, miscellaneous, light, and entertaining; may include continuous sketches of a light and instructive nature. The aim is to increase the popularity and usefulness of the periodical. Example announced: a series of sketches entitled 'The Mountains of the Moon; or, Travels and Adventures of Hakim Ben Sheytan' — likely apocryphal but amusing and instructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for studying mind — preference for physiological method
rubrics_metrics.description: Two contrasted methods of studying mind are described: (1) the metaphysical method, which regards mind as an abstraction known only in consciousness and largely avoids corpuscular/organ studies; and (2) the physiological method, which regards mind as the endowment of an organic structure whose material conditions are of supreme importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical mental science should favor the physiological method: investigate the brain, its anatomy, functions and diseases (anatomist, physiologist, pathologist), and ground psychological inquiry in material/organic conditions rather than pure metaphysical abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical conditions for mental growth and education
rubrics_metrics.description: When treating mental growth (a topic at the root of education), the physiological perspective holds that material conditions — ventilation, exercise, clothing, and diet — are fundamental conditions of successful work in education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educators should consider biological and nutritive conditions of the organism when cultivating the mind; these material concerns are central to psychological pedagogy rather than indifferent or irrelevant (contrary to metaphysical teachers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of insanity and suicide — treat as corporeal, causal phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Insanity and suicide should be regarded as phenomena with corporeal bases — derangements or morbidities of the brain — and thus approachable scientifically rather than as merely metaphysical problems or results of moral choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study these phenomena by seeking dynamic and causal explanations tied to organic/physical conditions. Suicide in particular is described as showing regularities and orderly variation corresponding to external conditions (climate, season, country), and demographic/social factors (age, sex, race, cultivation, social circumstances). Recognize an infinite series of cerebral morbidities from weakness to confirmed melancholia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive rule for Hebrew concrete numerals (biblical ages)
rubrics_metrics.description: In reading concrete numbers the Hebrews gave the larger number first (e.g., 'ninety and seven' for ninety-seven; 'forty and seven' for forty-seven). The reversal of this rule in translations produces incorrect large ages for patriarchs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators and revisers should correct cases where the order is reversed (e.g., Genesis v), and should observe that pluralizing certain numerals does not necessarily multiply by ten in every case (example discussion of 'mathim' for one hundred). Applying these corrections substantially reduces apparent disparities in patriarchal ages and resolves many objections based on inflated numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright status criterion for collected works (example: Irving's works)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all materials titled or offered as an author's 'works' are necessarily wholly in the public domain: latest writings and the only revised and authorized issues of earlier volumes remain protected by copyright, while some earlier unrevised magazine articles may have entered the public domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal judgments about publication depend on the specific material contained in the contested volume. Labeling or marketing a collection as an author's 'works' when it contains different or unrevised material can be misleading and may injure rights-holders, though courts may find legal grounds for restraint insufficient depending on facts. Editors/contributors should be precise about which texts are copyrighted (revised/authorized editions) versus which earlier periodical items have lapsed.
